The user just reported that the logo in the hero section looks “smushed.” I need to investigate why the logo is being rendered incorrectly after my recent edits. The HTML and CSS for the hero and the logo are already loaded in the file; I’ve just inspected the relevant CSS rules (the `.hero-logo` block) and confirmed the positioning and display logic. However, the visual distortion could be due to the image itself being resized improperly, or perhaps a missing or broken image asset causing the browser to fall back to a placeholder that looks squashed.

To diagnose this properly, I need to see the rendered page as a browser would. The most reliable way is to take a screenshot of the page (or at least the hero section) using an automated headless browser. That will let me confirm whether the logo is truly squashed in the layout or if it’s an artifact of my terminal view. 

Before I can run a screenshot script, I must ensure that a suitable browser executable is available in the environment. The Playwright library (which is likely already a dependency given the presence of `groq-paperclip-adapter` that often works with Playwright) can drive Chromium, Chrome, or Firefox. I don’t know which of these binaries are installed on the VM. Therefore, the next logical step is to query the system for the presence of common browser executables (`chromium`, `chromium-browser`, `google-chrome`, `firefox`). Additionally, Playwright stores its browser binaries under `~/.cache/ms-playwright`; checking that directory will tell me if Playwright has already downloaded a browser bundle that I can invoke.

Thus, I will run a Bash command that checks for any of those executables with `which` and also lists the contents of the Playwright cache directory. This will give me the information I need to decide which browser to launch for the screenshot step. No other actions are needed right now; once I know the available browser, I can write a small Playwright script to capture the hero section and examine the logo rendering.

The appropriate tool call is a Bash execution with the command:
`which chromium chromium-browser google-chrome firefox 2>/dev/null; ls ~/.cache/ms-playwright 2>/dev/null`

This will safely report the paths (or lack thereof) without causing errors, and the output will guide the next move.
